title: Capturing Homogeneous Influence among Students: Hypergraph Cognitive Diagnosis for Intelligent Education Systems

problem.claim: Cognitive diagnosis aims to infer students' proficiency levels on each knowledge concept from student-exercise interactions.

gap.claim: Existing methods struggle to capture homogeneous influence, causing substantially varying inferred proficiency levels for students with similar exercise performance and creating interpretability and efficacy shortcomings.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes HyperCDM, a hypergraph cognitive diagnosis model for capturing homogeneous influence.
HyperCDM learns student, exercise, and knowledge representations in separate hypergraphs and interconnects them through a feature-based interaction function.
HyperCDM uses an auto-encoder and K-means to construct hypergraphs from sparse response logs and uses momentum hypergraph convolution to mitigate over-smoothing.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On offline and online real-world datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance in interpretability and effective capture of homogeneous influence, with competitive generalization.
The authors report that ablation studies verify the efficacy of each component.
The authors report that a case study showcases homogeneous influence captured by HyperCDM.

narrative_sequence.summary: Cognitive diagnosis is framed as an upstream task for intelligent education systems that infers concept proficiency from student-exercise interactions.

Existing methods inadequately capture homogeneous influence, while hypergraph modeling is motivated by its ability to represent high-order similarity; incorporation still faces distortion, sparsity, and over-smoothing challenges.
HyperCDM addresses these challenges through separate hypergraphs, feature-based interconnection, response-log preprocessing and clustering, and momentum hypergraph convolution.
The authors report results from offline and online real-world datasets, ablations, and a case study.

source_observation.claim: When the target phenomenon involves high-order similarity, hypergraph modeling may provide a suitable representation.

interpretation.claim: Representation choice should reflect the relational structure of the phenomenon being modeled.

application.claim: Consider hypergraph-based representations for domains where group-level or high-order similarity is central.

exception.claim: Hypergraph adoption may still require explicit treatment of distortion, sparsity, and over-smoothing.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the datasets, sample sizes, metrics, baselines, or numerical results.
The abstract does not specify how homogeneous influence is operationalized or how interpretability is measured.
The abstract does not provide implementation details or evidence beyond the authors' reported experiments, ablation, and case study.
